item.title: North Korea reviews Switzerland relations after sanctions on youth camp linked to war
item.description:
North Korea reviews Switzerland relations after sanctions on youth camp linked to war
North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last monthByKIM TONG-HYUNG Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 2:34 AM
Share
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea threatened Tuesday to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, condemning Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a youth camp in eastern North Korea over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russia-occupied areas of Ukraine.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, described the Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan as an “open hostile act” and a “serious infringement” of the North’s sovereignty, according to a statement carried by state media.
Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials, said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia. She didn't directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated.
North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for economic assistance and military technology transfers.
Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he positions North Korea as part of a united front against the United States.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” North Korean state media said at the time.

item.title: South Africa convicts Zimbabwean who tried to travel to Russia to fight against Ukraine
item.description:
South Africa convicts Zimbabwean who tried to travel to Russia to fight against Ukraine
A Zimbabwean man has been convicted in South Africa of trying to travel to Russia to fight in its war against UkraineByMOGOMOTSI MAGOME Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 10:50 AM
JOHANNESBURG -- A Zimbabwean man was convicted and sentenced on Tuesday for trying to travel to Russia to fight in its war against Ukraine after being arrested in South Africa with eight others earlier this month.
Tafadzwa Sithole was sentenced to five years in prison, suspended for five years, and he is set to be deported back to Zimbabwe.
He told a South African court that he had agreed to fight for Russia in the war in exchange for “remuneration” after successfully applying online in Zimbabwe.
Sithole said a person he identified as “Albina” contacted him after he submitted the application, arranged accommodation in South Africa and provided a flight ticket to Russia.
His admissions were detailed in a plea agreement with South African prosecutors. He pleaded guilty to violating the Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which prohibits mercenary activity and regulates military assistance to parties in foreign conflicts, including recruitment and training.
The law also applies to foreign nationals.
Sithole, who described himself as an unemployed third-year student at a university in Zimbabwe, appeared in court with four other accused who are also negotiating plea agreements with prosecutors.
He said he entered South Africa legally on Nov. 4 and stayed in accommodation in Kempton Park, east of Johannesburg, in preparation for his travel to Russia.
He was arrested at O.R. Tambo International Airport on Nov. 8 while attempting to board a flight to Russia.

item.title: Houthi rebels close in on Aden as Yemeni forces dig in behind a fortified line
item.description:
Houthi rebels close in on Aden as Yemeni forces dig in behind a fortified line
Iran-backed Houthi rebels have advanced close to Yemen's government seat in AdenBySAM METZ Associated Press, SALLY ABOU ALJOUD Associated Press, and MENELAOS HADJICOSTIS Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 5:34 AM
Share
Iran-backed Houthi rebels have advanced to within about 60 kilometers (about 40 miles) of the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the southern city of Aden, but the forces fighting them have set up a fortified line to defend the city, a military official said Tuesday.
Iran reiterated Tuesday that it would not hold talks with the United States to end their conflict unless several conditions are met. It also said three oil tankers had struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire despite U.S. aerial protection.
Meanwhile, at least nine Palestinians were killed in several Israeli strikes in Gaza, local officials said.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Read our full coverage here.
The Houthis' advance toward Aden has come after forces allied with the government withdrew from areas on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, allowing the Houthis to consolidate their grip on territory around the crucial waterway.
Col. Majed al-Nuzaily, spokesman for the Yemeni army, said the forces that withdrew from the western coast are now stationed north and west of Aden “on a defense line built to stop the Houthi advance," as the rebels come within 60 kilometers of the city.
“Aden is a red line. It was a red line in 2015, when the Houthis came to the city and its people drove them out,” he said during a virtual briefing.
Speaking in the same briefing, Yemeni foreign ministry official Marwan al-Noman called for the United States and other Western countries to support the Yemeni coast guard in its efforts to intercept smuggled weapons to the Houthis, as well as provide training to Yemeni forces fighting the rebels on the ground.

item.title: Canada's defense minister says his country answers to no one in Washington
item.description:
Canada's defense minister says his country answers to no one in Washington
Canada’s defense minister says that his country answers to no one in Washington, asserting Canadian sovereignty after the Pentagon accused Ottawa of failing to meet its military commitmentsByROB GILLIES Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 12:58 PM
Share
TORONTO -- Canada’s defense minister said on Tuesday that his country answers to no one in Washington, asserting Canadian sovereignty a day after the Pentagon accused Ottawa of failing to do enough to defend North America.
The Pentagon said Canada lacked a credible plan to meet NATO’s spending targets, accusing Ottawa of relying for decades on American taxpayers to foot its defense bill. Relations between the two neighbors have been strained by U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.
“Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States,” Defense Minister David McGuinty told reporters.
He insisted Canada remains on track to spend 5% of gross domestic product on defense and related security investments by 2035, while emphasizing that NATO allies had agreed to review the spending pledge in 2029.
“We also said by 2029 we would be examining that 5% commitment,” McGuinty said.
McGuinty said Canada’s plans would bring spending to 4% of GDP by 2030, a “significant, significant step” from 1.25% of GDP 14 months ago.
NATO’s 2025 agreement calls for at least 3.5% of GDP for core defense and up to 1.5% for related security investments by 2035. The scheduled 2029 review will examine the pace and balance of spending against security threats and military needs.
The Pentagon’s unusually blunt fact sheet on Monday accused Ottawa of postponing its largest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”

item.title: Bangladesh's ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
item.description:
Bangladesh's ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return home from exile in India on Dec. 16ByJULHAS ALAM Associated PressNovember 23, 2026, 10:37 PM
DHAKA, Bangladesh -- DHAKA, Bangladesh (AP) — Sheikh Hasina, who was ousted as Bangladesh's prime minister more than two years ago, said Tuesday that she plans to return home from exile in India on Dec. 16, the day the country celebrates as Victory Day when it won independence after a war with Pakistan.
Hasina went into exile in India on Aug. 5, 2024, after a student-led mass uprising forced her to end her 15-year rule. She was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity involving the uprising in which hundreds of protesters were killed. Hasina rejected the verdict and has said she is ready to fight the case once she is back.
Abu Abdullah M Saleh, press secretary to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told The Associated Press that the government would stick to its position on Hasina's extradition as a convict.
“My government's stand is very clear. She has been convicted in a tribunal. We have sought her extradition,” he said by phone.
The junior minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters in a briefing on Tuesday that Hasina could return only “in handcuffs or under strict surveillance.”
“The reality is that no terrorist will ever be allowed to return this way without extradition,” he was quoted as saying by the country's leading English-language Daily Star newspaper.
It is expected that Hasina would be arrested upon her return and sent to jail.
A prosecutor had earlier said that Hasina wouldn't be able to appeal her death sentence as she missed the required deadline, and that there would be no legal basis to stop her execution.
In Bangladesh, presidential clemency is allowed, but Hasina has never sought that in earlier statements and has rejected the verdict outright.

item.title: Malaysia to repatriate another 6,803 Myanmar nationals despite ICJ genocide ruling
item.description:
Malaysia to repatriate another 6,803 Myanmar nationals despite ICJ genocide ruling
Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says the country plans to repatriate another 6,803 Myanmar nationals next monthByThe Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 4:45 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- Malaysia will repatriate another 6,803 Myanmar nationals next month, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Tuesday as he defended the government's engagement with Myanmar's military leadership, despite a landmark international court ruling finding the country responsible for genocide against Rohingya Muslims.
The International Court of Justice, based in The Hague, Netherlands, last week found Myanmar guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority, with evidence showing Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya in a 2017 military operation that included mass rapes and killings, and the destruction of thousands of homes.
Myanmar’s government has dismissed the ruling as unfair. Anwar told Parliament that Malaysia respected the ICJ's ruling, but would continue to engage Myanmar's leadership to facilitate the repatriation of refugees.
Malaysia hosts nearly 200,000 refugees from Myanmar, including Rohingya who fled a military crackdown and members of other ethnic minorities. Anwar said that efforts to resettle them in third countries had been unsuccessful and Malaysia couldn't continue bearing the burden indefinitely.
He said that talks with Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing, who visited Kuala Lumpur last month, had helped bring progress to the long-standing issue.
Another 1,500 people will be sent back on three Myanmar naval vessels on Dec. 6 and 7, while another 5,303 will return throughout next month by air, with all costs borne by Myanmar, Anwar said.
A total of 10,476 Myanmar nationals have already been repatriated this year, including 1,476 who were taken home aboard a Myanmar naval vessel on Sept. 29, he said.

item.title: Officials backtrack after 24-hour hunt for Istanbul lioness, saying she never existed
item.description:
Officials backtrack after 24-hour hunt for Istanbul lioness, saying she never existed
Turkish officials say a lioness that was subject to a 24-hour search and sparked panic among Istanbul residents does not actually existByThe Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 1:39 AM
Share
ISTANBUL -- A 24-hour search for a lioness in the Istanbul suburbs that sparked panic among local residents was thrown into fresh confusion late Monday when Turkish officials said the animal did not exist.
Istanbul’s governor mobilized teams of animal welfare experts, police and army commandos in the hunt for the lioness after it was “identified” – even releasing two videos of the animal prowling around the upmarket neighborhood of Uskumrukoy.
Residents were warned to stay home, and the 54-square-kilometer (about 20 square miles) Belgrade Forest to the north of Istanbul was sealed off.
By Monday evening, however, officials backtracked and said in a statement new images had been examined that showed the animal was “not a lion or any other large cat species.”
“The area has been scanned from the air with a drone equipped with thermal cameras and from the ground by our teams,” the statement said. “Baiting was also carried out and motion-sensor camera traps used."

item.title: Pope Francis' diary details profound spiritual crisis and encounters with the devil
item.description:
Pope Francis' diary details profound spiritual crisis and encounters with the devil
The Vatican has released excerpts of Pope Francis' private diaryByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 1:01 AM
Share
VATICAN CITY -- Pope Francis saw the “gates of hell” when he realized the depths of the clergy sexual abuse scandal and experienced mystical visions of the devil throughout his ministry, according to excerpts of his personal diary published Tuesday by the Vatican.
“The Private Diary of Pope Francis” also reveals the Argentine pope suffered a profound spiritual crisis in 2021-22, connected to his own temptations to exercise power omnipotently. He overcame the crisis by entrusting himself entirely to God’s mercy.
The book, released globally in several languages, offers a deeply personal view of Francis' mind and heart, revealing his innermost fears, insecurities, dreams and temptations. It shows him as incredibly hard on himself, lamenting his own sense of worthlessness and shame, and his utter trust in God to lead him, even from the depths of despair.
The book was curated by a close aide, Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, the Argentine theologian who heads the Vatican’s doctrine office and writes that Francis wanted the papers published. Fernández is listed as the author, as his comments contextualize Francis’ diary entries.
Written in a leather-bound calendar used as a notebook, it starts in 1992, when Jorge Mario Bergoglio was auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires. It continues through his time as cardinal in the Argentine capital and finally pope. The last entry is Aug. 18, 2024.
The most moving sections are Francis’ revelations of his own spiritual torments and what he described as encounters with the devil — visceral, tangible and seemingly terrifying visions. Two occurred in Buenos Aires, and the third after his disastrous 2018 trip to Chile.

item.title: Global land mine casualties hit a 5-year high, driven by Myanmar’s brutal civil war and Syria
item.description:
Global land mine casualties hit a 5-year high, driven by Myanmar’s brutal civil war and Syria
Casualties from land mines and unexploded ordnance reached a five-year high in 2025, with Southeast Asia seeing a significant number of those killed or woundedByDAVID RISING Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 3:14 AM
Share
BANGKOK -- Casualties from land mines or unexploded ordnance reached a five-year high in 2025, with Southeast Asia making up a disproportionate number of those killed or wounded, largely due to Myanmar's civil war, a report released Tuesday showed.
The annual global report by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines found civilians were the most affected, making up some 84% of the 6,929 casualties recorded in 2025, and half of them were children.
In Myanmar, where both government military forces and the militias fighting against them make widespread use of mines, 1,891 casualties were recorded in 2025, the highest number of any country for the third consecutive year.
“Myanmar has gone beyond crisis to catastrophe, and has claimed the ignoble title of top producer of land mine victims for a 3rd year in a row,” said Yeshua Moser-Puangsuwan, a co-author of the Landmine Monitor 2026 report. “There is now contamination at some level in almost 2/3 of the townships of the country.”
On average, five people are killed or wounded by land mines daily in Myanmar, the report found.
Driven by the Myanmar figures, Southeast Asia, where there is also widespread mine contamination in Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and elsewhere, accounted for 27% of global casualties in 2025 despite having just over 8% of the world's population.
Syria, which experienced a large-scale return of civilians after the fall of the Assad government at the end of 2024, saw a spike of more than 50% to 1,602 casualties in 2025, a testament to the ongoing dangers of mines and leftover ordnance even after fighting has stopped.

item.title: Hanoi eatery blast kills 6 and injures more than a dozen
item.description:
Hanoi eatery blast kills 6 and injures more than a dozen
An explosion suspected to be from a gas leak at a hot pot eatery in Hanoi has six people and injured more than a dozen othersByThe Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 2:51 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
HANOI, Vietnam -- An explosion at a hot pot eatery in Vietnam's capital on Tuesday, suspected to have been caused by a gas leak, killed six people, injured more than a dozen others and damaged nearby houses.
VnExpress, an online news outlet, said that the early morning blast in Hanoi shattered windows, cracked walls and tore metal shutters from their frames, while corrugated roofs and awnings collapsed. The report said that the explosion damaged nearby houses and shook neighboring apartment buildings, with debris scattered across the street.
Police are using detection equipment to search for survivors and hydraulic machinery to lift concrete slabs, amid concerns that more people may be trapped under the rubble as the eatery was packed when the blast struck, the report said. Authorities have also relocated residents from neighboring buildings deemed structurally unsafe, it said.
Hanoi police were cited as saying that investigations were ongoing. But preliminary findings pointed to a gas explosion that brought down part of the building. More than 14 people, including one with a traumatic brain injury, have been hospitalized, the report said.
